questions.prompt: A salt dissolves readily while the insulated solution becomes cooler. How can dissolution still be thermodynamically favorable under the conditions?
options: Every favorable dissolution must release heat
Cooling proves no ions entered solution
The salt must have a negative absolute entropy
A favorable entropy contribution can outweigh the positive enthalpy change.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Endothermic dissolution can be favorable when−TΔS is sufficiently negative. A is incorrect: enthalpy alone does not determine free-energy favorability. B is incorrect: temperature decrease is compatible with endothermic dissolution. C is incorrect: the relevant quantity is the net entropy change, not a required negative absolute value.

questions.prompt: What is the enthalpic effect of separating oppositely charged ions from their attractive crystal lattice, considered as one step of a dissolution model?
options: Energy is necessarily released in this separation step
Energy is required, giving a positive contribution.
It has no energy cost because the crystal is electrically neutral overall
It is identical to forming ion-water attractions
questions.explanation: B is correct. Overcoming attractive ion-ion interactions costs energy. A is incorrect: breaking attractive interactions requires input. C is incorrect: net neutrality does not remove strong local attractions. D is incorrect: lattice separation and hydration are distinct model steps.

questions.prompt: When separated ions form attractive interactions with surrounding polar water molecules, what is the usual enthalpic contribution of that interaction-formation step?
options: Positive solely because the ions are charged
Exactly zero for every ion
Negative, because forming favorable ion-water attractions releases energy.
It must equal the entire dissolution enthalpy
questions.explanation: C is correct. Hydration can offset the energy cost of separating lattice and solvent interactions. A is incorrect: charge supports attractive hydration rather than determining a positive formation cost. B is incorrect: different ions have substantial, different hydration energies. D is incorrect: other steps also contribute.

questions.prompt: Why can solvent reorganization oppose the entropy gain from dispersing a salt into ions?
options: Water molecules can become more constrained in hydration arrangements around ions.
All water molecules disappear chemically on contact with salt
Dissolved ions cannot move
Entropy counts only solute particles and excludes solvent
questions.explanation: A is correct. Local solvent ordering can contribute negatively to entropy even while solute particles disperse. B is incorrect: hydration does not consume all solvent. C is incorrect: hydrated ions still move. D is incorrect: the total solution change includes solvent arrangements.

questions.prompt: A student claims every ionic dissolution must have positive ΔS because the number of separated ions increases. What correction is needed?
options: Every dissolution must instead have negative ΔS
Include both solute dispersal and solvent reorganization before assigning the net sign.
Ion count directly gives the exact entropy change in joules per kelvin
Only the crystal color determines ΔS
questions.explanation: B is correct. Competing contributions can make total entropy change smaller or even negative. A is incorrect: that is another unjustified universal claim. C is incorrect: molecular arrangements and solvent effects require more information. D is incorrect: color is not a general entropy measure.

questions.prompt: At298 K, a specified dissolution has ΔH°=+15.0 kJ/mol and ΔS°=+80.0 J mol−1 K−1. What is ΔG°?
options: +38.84 kJ/mol
+15.0 kJ/mol
−23825 kJ/mol
−8.84 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: D is correct. 15.0−298(0.0800)=−8.84; the favorable entropy term outweighs endothermic enthalpy. A is incorrect: that adds TΔS rather than subtracting it. B is incorrect: that ignores entropy. C is incorrect: that combines joules and kilojoules without conversion.

questions.prompt: A dissolution model gives ΔH°=−25.0 kJ/mol and ΔS°=−120 J mol−1 K−1 at298 K. Which result shows why exothermicity alone is insufficient?
options: ΔG°=+10.8 kJ/mol, because the entropy penalty outweighs heat release.
ΔG°=−60.8 kJ/mol
ΔG° must be negative whenever ΔH° is negative
ΔG°=0 for all dissolutions
questions.explanation: A is correct. −25.0−298(−0.120)=+10.76 kJ/mol under standard conditions. B is incorrect: that adds the signed entropy term rather than subtracting it. C is incorrect: the entropy term can oppose it. D is incorrect: dissolution free energies depend on the substance and conditions.

questions.prompt: A simplified enthalpy ledger for dissolution lists lattice separation+700 kJ/mol, solvent rearrangement+20 kJ/mol, and ion-solvent interaction formation−725 kJ/mol. What is the net dissolution enthalpy?
options: +1445 kJ/mol
−725 kJ/mol
−5 kJ/mol
+25 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: C is correct. Adding all stated contributions gives700+20−725=−5. A is incorrect: that treats the favorable negative interaction term as positive. B is incorrect: that omits both positive contributions. D is incorrect: that reverses the sign of the lattice-plus-hydration subtotal and omits the +20 solvent term.

questions.prompt: Why is a large lattice-separation energy alone insufficient to rank the solubility of two salts?
options: Hydration, solvent reorganization and entropy contributions can differ and offset the lattice cost.
Lattice energy has no physical effect at all
Both salts must have identical ion-water interactions
The salt with the larger formula mass is always more soluble
questions.explanation: A is correct. Overall free energy depends on the combined contributions, not one isolated model step. B is incorrect: it contributes, but is not the whole balance. C is incorrect: different ions can interact differently with solvent. D is incorrect: formula mass alone does not determine the free-energy balance.

questions.prompt: A dissolving salt produces a substantial temperature decrease. What further thermodynamic information is needed to judge standard favorability from ΔH°−TΔS°?
options: Only the size of the stirring rod
The entropy change and the absolute temperature.
Only whether individual ions have positive or negative charge
No further information; cooling proves the standard process is unfavorable
questions.explanation: B is correct. Knowing only endothermic enthalpy does not establish the sign of the free-energy change. A is incorrect: it does not supply the missing entropy term. C is incorrect: charge signs alone do not give total entropy change. D is incorrect: an entropy-driven dissolution can be favorable.

questions.prompt: Stirring makes a salt reach its saturated concentration faster at the same controlled temperature. What conclusion is justified?
options: Ksp must increase in proportion to stirring speed
The hydration enthalpy must become zero
All salts become infinitely soluble if stirred long enough
The approach rate increased; equilibrium solubility need not change.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Mixing improves transport but does not itself change the fixed-temperature dissolution free-energy balance. A is incorrect: transport rate is not an equilibrium constant. B is incorrect: stirring does not erase ion-water interaction energies. C is incorrect: finite equilibrium solubility remains a thermodynamic constraint.
